content.title: About
content.content: Trout is a freshwater fish of the salmon family, inhabiting rivers and lakes in temperate climates. In Russia and CIS countries it is often labeled “NFS” (New Freshness), highlighting its clean taste and high nutrient content. Trout has delicate pink flesh, a moderately fatty flavor, and a characteristic aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Trout can change sex during its lifetime depending on environmental conditions.
Unlike many salmonids, trout usually does not migrate to the ocean and lives its whole life in fresh water.
The largest recorded trout weighed over 20 kg, though typical specimens are 1–3 kg.
Trout is widely farmed in aquaculture where water temperature is kept at 10‑16 °C for optimal flavor.
In Japan, trout is often prepared as “sabay” – a smoked‑salty delicacy.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Trout provides EPA and DHA – polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart and brain health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: 100 g of trout delivers about 20 g of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Trout is a good source of B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The fish contains selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, supporting immunity, bone health, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Low mercury content
items.content: Compared with large oceanic predators, trout has minimal levels of heavy metals.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including trout.

items.title: Parasite contamination
items.content: Raw or undercooked trout can harbor parasites; cooking to an internal temperature of 63 °C is recommended.

items.title: Sodium in smoked trout
items.content: Smoked trout often contains added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Environmental considerations
items.content: Improper aquaculture practices can lead to water pollution and antibiotic use.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Trout can be grilled, baked, boiled, or pan‑fried. It is commonly served with lemon, herbs (dill, parsley) and a light sauce. Smoked trout is used in salads, sandwiches, and appetizers. Raw trout (sashimi) is popular in Japanese cuisine but requires strict quality control.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh trout should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or an airtight container, and used within 2 days. Frozen trout can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Before cooking, check the smell: the fish should have a fresh, mild scent without ammonia notes.
